To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) women with long term multiple social roles reported relatively good health in mid-life, and this was not fully explained by early health, 2) women with long-term weak labour market ties were more likely to report being obese in mid-life and this was partly explained by early health selection, and 3) the long-term homemakers were heavier than other women from an early age, but they were more likely to have gained weight with age than other women
the relations between social roles in mid-life and self reported health at 54 years of age are largely explained by health selection, but not for obesity at 53 years of age.

women with weak long term labour market ties were more likely to have obesity at age 54, and this was not due to early health selection, but was probably due to the accumulation of health risk factors associated with long term homemaking, including a high BMI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of social roles on health and the role of health in the formation of social roles.
the role of social roles in the production of health and ill health.
the relationship between social roles and self reported health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women’s long term social role history is related to mid-life health, but the direction of causation is unclear.

the relation between social roles and self reported health in mid-life is largely explained by causation but that the relation between employment and obesity in mid-life is partly explained by causation and partly explained by health selection.
the health of women in midlife is not explained by health selectivity into social roles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the health of women who have weak long term ties with the labour market may deteriorate over the life course, and this may contribute to the higher mortality rates observed among women who have weak ties with the labour markets.

the relations between social roles (employment and family roles) and health are complex and not easily explained by a single mechanism, but that the effects of social roles on women’s health are generally small.
social roles are important for health, and that women who have weak ties to the labour force are more likely to have health problems in mid-life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social roles are associated with health independently of early health and that these associations may change over the life course.
the relations between social roles (work and parenthood) and health are not explained by early life health.
social roles are associated with health in mid-life, and that these associations are not fully explained by early health, although early health may contribute to some associations.
